title: Wanting to revise is not a plan

source.citation: Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119. The technique was introduced in Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493-503.
source.finding: Across 94 independent tests, people who made 'if situation X, then I will do Y' plans were more likely to act on their goals than people who only held the goal.
source.caveat: Most of the 94 studies involved adults and short-term goals, not teenagers revising. The effect in everyday life is likely smaller than the headline average.

scenes.narration: Wanting to revise more doesn't make you revise more.
I'll do more maths this week. That's a goal. It has no time and no place. So it loses to everything else.
A psychologist called Peter Gollwitzer tested a fix. It's called an if-then plan.
If it's four o'clock, then I open my maths book at the kitchen table.
Across ninety-four studies, people who made plans like that followed through more often.
Today, write one sentence. If it's this time, then I do this, in this place. Stick it where you'll see it.
